sections.html:
• Name: Vampire Crab (also Vampire, Geosesarma sb)
  • Scientific name: Geosesarma dennerle
  • Type: semi-terrestrial crab
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres
  • Keeping: easy to medium; breeding: difficult
  • Carapace size: 1.5–2.5 cm; size across the leg span: 5 cm
  • Aquarium type: paludarium (an aquarium with both terrestrial and aquatic elements, freshwater)
  • KH: 0–10; GH: 4–16
  • Humidity: 75% and higher
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 2 years
  • Colour form: purple with orange eyes

Vampire crabs (Geosesarma dennerle) are relatively new to the hobby, but have become increasingly popular as ornamental species in recent years. The ecology and biology of Geosesarma species is still poorly studied, so there is a lot of wrong information or confusion about caring for them.

Vampire crabs are not freshwater crabs, they are semi-terrestrial animals. They are sociable, omnivorous, pretty hardy and easy to care for.

They were first introduced in 2006. Since then, an increasing number of colourful land-dwelling crabs have been sold for the ornamental fish trade in Europe, Asia and America under the name "Vampire crabs". According to Christian Lukhaup, these species have been in the aquarium trade for many years but no one knew where they came from.

The genus Geosesarma includes a group of semi-terrestrial crabs widely distributed in Southeast Asia, the eastern Indian Ocean and the western Pacific. It currently contains 58 recognised species, and taxonomy at the genus level is still in a state of flux.

The two most common and popular colour forms are a bicolored cream and violet morph (Vampire crab) and a bicolored dark brown and bright orange one (Red devil crab).

There are several theories on why they are called Vampire crabs. According to the first, it is because of their glowing yellow eyes and creamy spots on the back that can have a bat-like shape. The second says there is no mystery and it is simply good marketing, because catchy names attract attention.

They come from Sulawesi, Java, Krakatau or the Riau Islands. The species Geosesarma hagen (Red devil crab) and Geosesarma dennerle (Vampire crab) were named after the German company Dennerle and Rolf C. Hagen, who supported the study in Java.

Geosesarma dennerle (and Geosesarma hagen) share the same natural habitat. They live in forests, between rocks and among dense vegetation, near freshwater rivers and lakes. They do not depend on saltwater for development.

In nature, Vampire crabs live in leaf litter and rotten wood near streams. The species inhabits forest with pure, fresh, running rivers and streams.

They do not require anything big. Several Vampire crabs (1 male and 2 females) can be kept in a 20-litre tank. To increase the colony, a tank of at least 40 litres is better.

Floor space is more important than height. These crabs are great escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Keeping Vampire crabs is easy if you know how to care for them the right way.

Land vs water ratio

Vampire crabs require more land than water (paludarium), so they are not suitable for freshwater tanks. A common mistake is believing that rocks and driftwood to climb and sit on are enough. To give them an environment where they can thrive and breed, mimic their natural habitat. An 80/20 setup of land and water (or at least 50/50) is preferable. They stay longer on land than in water and do not need a lot of water, as long as water pools can completely cover their entire bodies. Ideally, the paludarium should contain a 10–15 cm deep bottom tray with freshwater.

Vampire crabs cannot stay in water for a long time and will drown. It is crucial to provide a variety of surfaces for them to get out of the water.

Clean water

Vampire crabs need clean water for moulting and breeding. If no filter is used, replace the water regularly and do not let it sit in the tank for ages. Every time you replace water, use Seachem Prime to dechlorinate it, as chlorine is dangerous for them. Depending on the setup, an external canister filter can be a good choice; in that case remineralise the water with Salty Shrimp GH/KH+ or GH+.

Substrate

The substrate should be gravel, earth, sand or a sand-earth mixture, for them to nibble at and excavate in.

Decorations and plants

They appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, wood, plants, PVC pipes, etc. They do not eat healthy plants and can be kept in well-planted setups. They can benefit from live plants by collecting bacteria and microorganisms off them.

Vampire crabs thrive in water with a pH of 7.5–8.0. If the pH is too low they become very lethargic. The ideal temperature is around 24–28°C, KH 0–10 and GH 4–16.

They also need stable humidity of around 75% or higher. This is one of the reasons why people fail to keep them.

Vampire crabs are predominantly omnivorous and can eat almost anything. In the wild, their diet consists of small terrestrial insects (living and dead crickets, grasshoppers, earthworms, mealworms, woodlice and springtails), worms and plant detritus. In captivity, in addition to any organic matter (brine shrimp, earthworm pieces, bloodworms, etc.), they eat all kinds of dried algae, shrimp or fish flakes, wafers, pellets, vegetables (dried or fresh), dry leaves, etc.

Like all snails, shrimp and crayfish, crabs require a lot of calcium for their exoskeleton.

Vampire crabs are scavengers and will eat nearly anything on the tank floor.

Like most Geosesarma species, Vampire crabs are nocturnal and shy, although from time to time they are seen at dusk or even during the day.

They are small, barely reaching 5 cm across the leg span, with a carapace about 2.5 cm wide. The claws do not open very wide, so it is very hard for them even to pinch you. Their spectacular colours (bright purple claws, yellow eyes and a violet-purple to purplish-brown carapace with a cream to yellowish-white spot on the back) explain their attraction to aquarists.

They are generally peaceful among each other, but not with crabs of a different kind. For example, Geosesarma hagen (Red devil crab) and Geosesarma dennerle (Vampire crab) kept together will fight more often. Biologists believe this is because in the wild they occupy the same space at the same time.

They are not very active. Once they find a place they like, they stay there for long periods, but they can sprint short distances very well.

Vampire crabs are social animals that do well in a group of their own kind. If you keep other Geosesarma species (such as Tangerine-head crab, Red devil crab) or Metasesarma species (such as Red apple crab, Marble crab) in the same tank, be ready for conflicts and territorial disputes. Vampire crabs will lose the fights most times.

If you keep shrimp and fish with them, there will be losses from time to time. Because of predation, it is not advisable to keep them with small snails at all.

Moulting

Like other crustaceans, the Vampire crab has a hard exoskeleton that prevents growth, so to grow it has to shed the old shell and grow a new, larger one. During the first 6 months of life they moult many times; this decreases to about once a month in adults.

Both moulting and breeding occur in freshwater. During and right after moulting, they are extremely vulnerable, so provide many hiding places or other crabs may eat a freshly moulted one.

• Males are slightly bigger than females.
  • Males have larger, brighter claws. Females have smaller claws (about half that size).
  • The underside of the male's shell (abdomen) is oblong or pointed. In females it is rounded (wider and oval).

Vampire crabs do not have any mating rituals. The male simply flips the female upside down and wraps himself around her to fertilise.

After mating, it takes about 1 month for the eggs to hatch. Before hatching, females become even more secretive and hide almost all the time. Depending on size, females can carry 20 to 80 eggs. The eggs are large and development is direct (no larval stages).

Females give birth to live, fully formed miniatures of the adult, and release the young into freshwater. Freshly hatched young are only 1–2 mm long. They cannot live separately from the mother and stay with her (still under the abdomen) for up to several weeks.

Cannibalism can occur once brood-care behaviour ends, so it is advisable to separate the mother from the baby crabs. Otherwise, only a small number will reach adulthood. Young crabs can also become prey to their siblings during moulting, so provide as many hiding places as possible and ideally separate them by size.
